questions.question: Maya's tally table has 4 rows, one for each equal part of her spinner: red, blue, green and yellow. After her experiment the table shows 4 tally marks beside red, 3 beside blue, 5 beside green and 0 beside yellow. How many times did Maya spin the spinner in all?
options: 12 spins
13 spins
4 spins
5 spins
questions.explain: The total number of trials is the sum of every row: 4 + 3 + 5 + 0 = 12 spins. A row with 0 marks still belongs in the table, but it adds nothing — do not add 1 for it, and do not just report the biggest row.

questions.question: Jae rolls a die and records each roll in a tally table. In the row for the number 3 he has one full group of five (four upright marks crossed by one slanted mark) and then 2 more single marks. How many times did Jae roll a 3?
options: 6 times
7 times
5 times
2 times
questions.explain: A crossed group stands for 5, so count 5 + 2 = 7. The slanted mark is the fifth tally, not a decoration — counting only the four upright marks (giving 6) is the usual slip.

questions.question: Ella's tally table has 3 rows: blue, green and white. She plans 20 draws from a bag. She draws one marble, sees blue, and puts it back. What should she do next so her experiment is recorded properly?
options: Stop the experiment and say blue is the most likely colour, because blue came out first.
Finish all 20 draws first, then try to remember every colour and fill in the table at the end.
Make one tally mark in the blue row right away, then draw the next marble.
Make a tally mark only if she draws blue two times in a row.
questions.explain: In an experiment you record each outcome with one tally mark as soon as it happens, then repeat the trial. Deciding after a single draw, or trusting your memory until the end, is how results get lost.

questions.question: Noah tosses a coin and keeps a tally table with a heads row and a tails row. The heads row has 2 full groups of five plus 1 single mark. The tails row has 1 full group of five plus 4 single marks. How many tosses does his table record altogether?
options: 11 tosses
17 tosses
22 tosses
20 tosses
questions.explain: Heads is 5 + 5 + 1 = 11 and tails is 5 + 4 = 9, so the experiment has 11 + 9 = 20 trials. Adding only one row, or counting a crossed group as 4, gives the wrong total.

questions.question: At recess in Kelowna, Amir spins a spinner with 6 equal parts and tallies every spin. He spins 30 times in total. His table shows purple 6, orange 5, white 4, black 3 and pink 4. The green row is smudged. How many spins should be in the green row?
options: 8 spins
22 spins
30 spins
12 spins
questions.explain: Add the rows you can read: 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 22, then subtract from the total, 30 − 22 = 8. The trap is stopping at 22 — that is what the other colours got, not what green got.

questions.question: Sofia's class did 17 spins of the 'weather' spinner and every spin landed on sun. Which description shows 17 recorded correctly with tally marks in the sun row?
options: One group of five and seven single marks
Three groups of five and two single marks
Seventeen groups of five
Three groups of five and seven single marks
questions.explain: Tally marks are bundled in fives: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, then 2 singles makes 17. Once you have five leftovers you must bundle them into a new group, so a record with seven singles left over is never right.

questions.question: Ravi wants to find out how often a 6 comes up when he rolls a fair die. Which plan records his experiment best?
options: Roll the die 5 times, see which number wins, and write that number in his notebook.
Guess how many 6s he will get and write that number in the table instead of rolling.
Roll the die 50 times, make one tally mark in the row for the number he rolls each time, then count the marks in the 6 row.
Roll the die 50 times but make a tally mark only when the number is different from the roll before it.
questions.explain: An experiment means doing many trials and tallying every single outcome, then counting the row you care about. Skipping trials, or replacing rolls with a guess, means the table no longer shows what really happened.

questions.question: Lin draws a cube from a bag, records it with a tally mark and puts it back, 25 times in all. Her table shows red 9 and blue 7, and every other draw was yellow. How many more yellow draws than blue draws did she record?
options: 9 more
16 more
0 — the same number
2 more
questions.explain: First find yellow: 25 − 9 − 7 = 9 draws. Then compare: 9 − 7 = 2 more yellow than blue. The common slip is answering 9, which is the yellow count, not the difference.

questions.question: Nadia's spinner has 4 equal parts: red, blue, green and yellow. She spins it 8 times and her tally table shows green 5, red 1, blue 1, yellow 1. She says, 'Green must take up more of this spinner.' What is the best thing to say about her claim?
options: She cannot tell yet; 8 spins is very few, so she should keep spinning and tallying many more trials.
She is right — green got 5 out of 8, so green must be the biggest part.
The spinner is broken and the class should throw it out.
Green is certain to come up on her next spin as well.
questions.explain: The four parts are equal, so each colour is equally likely; a short experiment can still look lopsided by chance. The classic mistake is judging a spinner from only a handful of trials — more trials make the tallies even out.

questions.question: Sam and Priya each test the same bag of counters at their Surrey school. Sam draws 10 times and tallies his results. Priya draws 100 times and tallies hers. Whose tally table gives a better idea of what is inside the bag?
options: Sam's, because 10 marks are quicker to count than 100.
Priya's, because more trials give a more trustworthy picture of the bag.
Sam's, because he finished first and one colour clearly won his 10 draws.
Neither — an experiment can never tell you anything about what is in a bag.
questions.explain: The more trials you run and tally, the closer the results get to what the bag really holds. A small number of draws can easily give a 'clear winner' by luck, which is why 10 draws is weaker evidence than 100.

questions.question: A Grade 4 class spun a 4-colour spinner 30 times and took turns tallying. At the end their table shows red 8, blue 7, green 6 and yellow 5. Which statement about their experiment is true?
options: Red is the most likely colour, because 8 marks out of 26 is the biggest share.
The spinner must be unfair, because the four rows are not equal.
The rows add to 26, so 4 spins were never tallied and the table is incomplete.
The table is fine as it is, because 26 is close enough to 30.
questions.explain: Always check that the tally rows add up to the number of trials: 8 + 7 + 6 + 5 = 26, but they spun 30 times, so 4 spins were missed. A table that does not match the number of trials cannot be used to draw any conclusion about the spinner.

questions.question: Priya's spinner has 2 equal parts, red and white. She predicts about half the spins will be red. She spins 20 times and her tally shows red 12 and white 8. What is the best conclusion?
options: The spinner is tilted toward red, because red beat white.
Red is twice as likely as white on this spinner.
She must have tallied wrong, because a fair spinner has to give exactly 10 and 10.
Her results are close to her prediction; experiment results wobble, and with more spins the two counts usually get closer to even.
questions.explain: With two equal parts, 12 and 8 out of 20 is a normal wobble around the predicted half — real experiment results rarely land exactly on the prediction. The trap is deciding the spinner is unfair (or that red is twice as likely) from one short run of trials.
